body:
Yes, I think most people would keep a consistent style between variable and member names, so would want the `camelcase` rule to warn them about these.

**edit:** Oh I see, you're interfacing with a library that does not use camel-case names. Interesting...

The problem is that there's no way for us to know what is an object that you define vs. an object being used from a library. There is literally no discriminating information in that regard. 

I think the real answer is to be able to programmatically turn off rules in section of code. That's what #320 is about. 

I'm open to other suggestions as well - at the moment I can't see a change to this rule that would make this easier.

@nzakas: Well, if the rules was split to two rules, checking identifier and member names separately, it would make it easier for someone to disable just the member name checking in the portion of the code that interacts with that library. I'm not sure if we should split the `camelcase` rule, though.

I wouldn't split the rule, mostly because I don't think it solves the
problem. If you're using an object that you wrote and one that you didn't,
the method names could have different formatting.

I would like to add an option to this rule to be able to specify
"variables", "properties", or "both". I think that would be useful.

I can understand the object member names, but is there no way to know that the `camelcase` is occurring with an actual function call?  If so I think maybe that ought never hit that rule.  If the `camelcase` is a function call in my own code, then that'll get caught when eslint is run over where the function is defined.  I don't need it to be caught where I call it too, ya?

That's an interesting point - we could definitely filter out function calls. The only real gap we would have then would be properties, because it's hard to know if the property is just being added or being overwritten. 

Keep in mind that function declarations within a code base can be separate from their uses, as well. This isn't just a third party library scenario. 

Other thoughts?

Yep, separate from their uses for sure, but I would expect the declaration to be the thing that hits me, not the usage.  Mostly.  If it's my own code base, it doesn't hurt if my eslint output lights up like a xmas tree because I'm using my own un-`camelcase`ed functions.  But I think its enough if it just reports the declaration.
I think you've convinced me. On properties we will still be stuck, but ah well.

repository.name: eslint
repository.description: Find and fix problems in your JavaScript code.

issue.body:
Previously, the rule would flag this:

``` js
foo.do_something();
```

As pointed out in #656, you're at the mercy of external libraries on function and method calls, and where we really should flag is on declaration of these identifiers. So this changes the rule such that it does not flag `CallExpression` identifiers.

issue.body:
Similar to #656, if you're reading a property value that has underscores in it, it shouldn't be your fault. A lot of web services do this, as well as libraries. So this should be okay:

``` js
var foo = bar.baz_boom;
```

This should still warn:

``` js
bar.baz_boom = "foo";
```

issue.body:
There are situations where third-party code or services are configured by calling a function with an object literal. Those objects are flagged the camelCase rule:

``` javascript
var snakes = require('somesnakelib');  // not my code
snakes({snake_prop: true});  // ESLint: "Identifier 'snake_prop' is not in camel case."
```

JSCS dealt with this by adding an [`ignoreProperties`](http://jscs.info/rules.html#requirecamelcaseoruppercaseidentifiers) option to their CamelCase rule. I like enforcing names and would rather not disable the CamelCase rule to use code that I don't control without errors. 

This was touched on in #656,  #672, #674 and #1550, but object literals are still being flagged.
